introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0775 Further Mathematics 1, June 2023, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one answer you score zero). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.
incertitudes: Le sujet est un scan sans couche texte, lu page par page en image (filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés). Aucune constante n'est nécessaire : toutes les réponses sont des valeurs exactes ou des formes algébriques.

Question 7 : dans la table imprimée, la dernière cellule de la quatrième ligne (colonne « (p ∨ q) ⇒ q ») est F, alors que F ⇒ F vaut V ; cette cellule n'intervient pas dans la question (a = F et b = F), la réponse D est conservée.

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 8, 17. Question 8 : la valeur exacte de l'intégrale est -2, absente des quatre options imprimées (-3, 0, 3, 6). Question 17 : l'énoncé imprimé « x + 1 = 3 » (sans barres de module visibles) rend vraies à la fois « at most one value », « at least one value » et « just one value » ; avec un module, seule « at least one value » serait vraie.

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac{x^2+1}{(1-x^2)}$, $x \neq \pm 1$, expressed in partial fractions where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The numerator and the denominator have the same degree, so the fraction is improper and a constant term must appear. Divide first: $\dfrac{x^2+1}{1-x^2} = -1 + \dfrac{2}{1-x^2}$. Then $\dfrac{2}{1-x^2} = \dfrac{2}{(1-x)(1+x)} = \dfrac{1}{1-x}+\dfrac{1}{1+x}$ (check: $\dfrac{(1+x)+(1-x)}{1-x^2} = \dfrac{2}{1-x^2}$). Hence $\dfrac{x^2+1}{1-x^2} = \dfrac{1}{1-x}+\dfrac{1}{1+x}-1$, that is $a=b=1$ with a constant $-1$. Options A and C have no constant term, so they tend to $0$ as $x\to\infty$ whereas the given fraction tends to $-1$; option B has $+1$ instead of $-1$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The integrating factor for the differential equation $x\dfrac{dy}{dx} - 2y = x^2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Put the equation in the standard form $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)$ by dividing by $x$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}-\dfrac{2}{x}y = x$, so $P(x) = -\dfrac{2}{x}$. The integrating factor is $e^{\int P\,dx} = e^{-2\ln|x|} = x^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{x^2}$. Check: multiplying by it gives $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{y}{x^2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{x}$, which is exactly integrable. The common trap is to use the coefficient $-2$ without dividing by $x$ first. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In exponential form, $1 - \tanh x \equiv$
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $\tanh x = \dfrac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{e^{x}+e^{-x}}$. Then $1-\tanh x = \dfrac{(e^{x}+e^{-x})-(e^{x}-e^{-x})}{e^{x}+e^{-x}} = \dfrac{2e^{-x}}{e^{x}+e^{-x}}$. Multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^{x}$ gives $\dfrac{2}{e^{2x}+1}$. Check with $x=0$: $1-\tanh0=1$ and $\dfrac{2}{1+1}=1$. Option A is $\dfrac{2e^{2x}}{e^{2x}+1}=1+\tanh x$, which has the wrong sign, and C and D are undefined at $x=0$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which one of the following functions has a removable discontinuity?
questions.corrige_markdown: A discontinuity is removable when the limit exists (finite) at the point where the function is undefined, which happens when the factor that vanishes in the denominator also cancels in the numerator. For C, $f(x)=\dfrac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1} = x+1$ for $x \neq 1$, so $\lim_{x\to1} f(x) = 2$ exists and defining $f(1)=2$ removes the discontinuity. In A, B and D the numerator does not vanish where the denominator does ($x=-1$: $2$; $x=1$: $2$; $x=3$: $18$), so each has a vertical asymptote (an infinite discontinuity), which cannot be removed. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The series $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{r^{k}}$ is convergent for
questions.corrige_markdown: This is the $p$-series with $p=k$. By the integral test, $\sum 1/r^{k}$ converges if and only if $\int_1^\infty x^{-k}\,dx$ converges, that is $\left[\dfrac{x^{1-k}}{1-k}\right]_1^\infty$ is finite, which needs $1-k<0$, i.e. $k>1$. For $k=1$ the series is the harmonic series $\sum 1/r$, which diverges (so $k \geq 1$ is wrong), and for $k<1$ the terms do not decrease fast enough. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The argument of the complex number $1 + e^{-2i\theta}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Factor out the half-angle: $1+e^{-2i\theta} = e^{-i\theta}\left(e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}\right) = 2\cos\theta\,e^{-i\theta}$. For $\cos\theta>0$ (that is $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}<\theta<\tfrac{\pi}{2}$) the modulus is $2\cos\theta$ and the argument is $-\theta$. (Check with $\theta = 0.4$: $1+e^{-0.8i} \approx 1.697 - 0.717i$, whose argument is $-0.4$.) The common error $-2\theta$ takes the argument of $e^{-2i\theta}$ alone and forgets the added $1$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the truth table below

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \vee q$ | $(p \vee q) \Rightarrow q$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T |
| T | F | T | a |
| F | T | T | T |
| F | F | b | F |

The truth values of a and b are respectively
questions.corrige_markdown: For $a$: the row has $p=T$, $q=F$, so $p\vee q = T$ and the implication $T \Rightarrow F$ is false: $a = F$. For $b$: the row has $p=F$, $q=F$, so $p\vee q = F\vee F = F$: $b = F$. Hence $(a,b) = (F,F)$. (The last cell printed in the fourth row, F, is not consistent with the truth table of an implication, since $F \Rightarrow F$ is true, but this cell does not enter the question, which only asks for $a$ and $b$.) **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Let $f(x) = [x]$, where $[x]$ is the greatest integer function. $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2} f(x)\,dx =$

*Options as printed:* A) $-3$   B) $0$   C) $3$   D) $6$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The greatest integer function is constant on each interval $[n, n+1)$, so split the integral: on $[-2,-1)$ $[x]=-2$, on $[-1,0)$ $[x]=-1$, on $[0,1)$ $[x]=0$, on $[1,2)$ $[x]=1$. Therefore $\int_{-2}^{2}[x]\,dx = (-2)(1)+(-1)(1)+0(1)+1(1) = -2$. This value is not among the printed options ($-3$, $0$, $3$, $6$), so no letter can be marked.

**Intended answer: $-2$ (no printed option matches this exact value).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

themes: mean and root mean square values
questions.enonce_markdown: The root mean square value of $\sin x$ in the interval $0 \leq x \leq \tfrac{1}{4}\pi$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a function on $[a,b]$ the root mean square value is $\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{b-a}\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx}$. Here $b-a=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so the r.m.s. value is $\sqrt{\dfrac{4}{\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin^2x\,dx} = 2\left[\dfrac{1}{\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin^2x\,dx\right]^{1/2}$, which is option C (the factor $4$ under the root becomes $2$ outside it). Option B would be correct for an interval of length $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$; A and D have no square root or the wrong factor. Numerically $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin^2x\,dx = \dfrac{\pi}{8}-\dfrac{1}{4}$, so the r.m.s. value is $\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{\pi}}\approx 0.426$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Cartesian equation of a curve whose polar equation is $r = 2a\cos\theta$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply the polar equation by $r$: $r^2 = 2a\,r\cos\theta$. With $r^2=x^2+y^2$ and $r\cos\theta = x$ this gives $x^2+y^2 = 2ax$, that is $x^2+y^2-2ax=0$, i.e. $(x-a)^2+y^2=a^2$, a circle of radius $a$ centred at $(a,0)$ (it passes through the pole and is symmetric about the initial line). Options B and D involve $y = r\sin\theta$ and C is the circle centred at $(-a,0)$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The coordinates of the focus of the parabola $y^2 = 16(x+1)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Compare with $Y^2 = 4aX$, where $Y=y$ and $X=x+1$. Then $4a=16$, so $a=4$. In the $(X,Y)$ frame the focus is $(a,0) = (4,0)$, that is $X=4$, $Y=0$, so $x = X-1 = 3$ and $y=0$. The focus is $(3,0)$ (vertex $(-1,0)$ plus $a=4$ to the right). Option A forgets the shift of the vertex. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $(\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{k})\times(2\mathbf{i}-\lambda\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}) = -4\mathbf{i}-7\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}$, the value of $\lambda$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Write the vectors in components: $(1,0,-4)\times(2,-\lambda,-1)$. Using the determinant rule, the $\mathbf{i}$ component is $0\cdot(-1)-(-4)(-\lambda) = -4\lambda$, the $\mathbf{j}$ component is $(-4)(2)-(1)(-1) = -7$, and the $\mathbf{k}$ component is $(1)(-\lambda)-0\cdot2 = -\lambda$. So the product is $-4\lambda\,\mathbf{i}-7\mathbf{j}-\lambda\mathbf{k}$. Equating with $-4\mathbf{i}-7\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}$ gives $\lambda=1$ (both the $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ components agree, and the $\mathbf{j}$ component $-7$ is a check). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A linear transformation, $T$, is defined as follows: $T:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$, $(x,y)\mapsto(x-2y,\,x+y)$. The Kernel of $T$ is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The kernel is the set of vectors that $T$ sends to the zero vector: $x-2y=0$ and $x+y=0$. Subtracting the equations gives $3y=0$, so $y=0$ and then $x=0$. The kernel is therefore the set containing only the zero vector of $\mathbb{R}^2$, written $\{(0,0)\}$. Option A is a single vector, not a set; C is a scalar; D, $\{0,0\}=\{0\}$, is a set containing the number $0$, not an element of $\mathbb{R}^2$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that $(\{a,b,c,d\},*)$ whose operation table is given below, is a group, then the identity element is

| $*$ | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ | $d$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $a$ | $b$ | $c$ | $d$ | $a$ |
| $b$ | $c$ | $d$ | $a$ | $b$ |
| $c$ | $d$ | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ |
| $d$ | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ | $d$ |
questions.corrige_markdown:
The identity $e$ satisfies $e*x = x*e = x$ for every element $x$, so its row and its column of the table must repeat the headings. The row of $d$ reads $d*a=a$, $d*b=b$, $d*c=c$, $d*d=d$ and the column of $d$ reads $a*d=a$, $b*d=b$, $c*d=c$, $d*d=d$. So $d$ is the identity. The other elements fail: for example $a*a=b
eq a$, $b*b=d
eq b$, $c*c=b
eq c$. (The group is cyclic of order 4, generated by $a$: $a, a^2=b, a^3=c, a^4=d$.) **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: How many distinct solutions are there to the congruence $12x \equiv 15 \pmod{21}$?
questions.corrige_markdown: The congruence $ax\equiv b \pmod n$ has solutions if and only if $d=\gcd(a,n)$ divides $b$, and then it has exactly $d$ solutions modulo $n$. Here $\gcd(12,21)=3$ and $3\mid15$, so there are $3$ solutions. Explicitly, divide by $3$: $4x\equiv5 \pmod 7$; since $4\times2=8\equiv1$, the inverse of $4$ is $2$ and $x\equiv10\equiv3 \pmod 7$. The solutions modulo $21$ are $x=3, 10, 17$ (check: $12\times3=36\equiv15$, $12\times10=120=5\times21+15$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The asymptotes to the curve $y=f(x)$, where $f(x) = x-1+\ln\left|\dfrac{x-2}{x-1}\right|$, are
questions.corrige_markdown: Vertical asymptotes occur where the argument of the logarithm tends to $0$ or $\infty$. As $x\to2$, $\left|\dfrac{x-2}{x-1}\right|\to0$ and $\ln\to-\infty$; as $x\to1$, the ratio $\to\infty$ and $\ln\to+\infty$. So $x=2$ and $x=1$ are both vertical asymptotes. As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\dfrac{x-2}{x-1}\to1$, so $\ln\left|\dfrac{x-2}{x-1}\right|\to0$ and $f(x)-(x-1)\to0$: the oblique asymptote is $y=x-1$. All three lines are asymptotes. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The statement $x+1=3$, is true for

*Options as printed:* A) all real values   B) at most one value   C) at least one value   D) just one value
questions.corrige_markdown:
As printed, the equation $x+1=3$ gives $x=2$ only, so it is true for exactly one value. The printed options are however not mutually exclusive: 'at most one value', 'at least one value' and 'just one value' are all true of a statement with exactly one solution. (If the left side was meant to be a modulus, $|x+1|=3$, the solutions would be $x=2$ and $x=-4$ and only 'at least one value' would be correct.) The question cannot be marked reliably with a single letter.

**Intended answer: D (just one value).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}-x, & x<0\\ 0, & x=0\\ x, & x>0.\end{cases}$ Which one of the following statements is true?
questions.corrige_markdown: This is the modulus function $f(x)=|x|$. For every $x$, $f(-x)=|-x|=|x|=f(x)$: if $x>0$ then $-x<0$ and $f(-x)=-(-x)=x=f(x)$, and $f(0)=0$. So $f$ is even and not odd ($f(-1)=1\neq-f(1)=-1$). It is continuous at $0$ since both one-sided limits equal $0=f(0)$, and it is not periodic because $f(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of $x$ for which $\sinh^{-1}(2x)=\ln 4$ is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Apply $\sinh$ to both sides: $2x=\sinh(\ln4) = \dfrac{e^{\ln4}-e^{-\ln4}}{2} = \dfrac{4-\tfrac14}{2} = \dfrac{15}{8}$. Hence $x=\dfrac{15}{16}$. (Check with the logarithmic form $\sinh^{-1}u=\ln\left(u+\sqrt{u^2+1}\right)$: for $u=\dfrac{15}{8}$, $\sqrt{u^2+1}=\dfrac{17}{8}$ and $\ln\left(\dfrac{15}{8}+\dfrac{17}{8}\right)=\ln4$.) Option B is the value of $2x$, a common slip. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A similarity transformation (similitude) $f$, on a complex plane is defined by $z'=(3-4i)z+1+i$. Its scale factor is
questions.corrige_markdown: A similitude $z'=az+b$ is a rotation through $\arg a$, an enlargement of scale factor $|a|$, and a translation by $b$. The scale factor is $|a|=|3-4i|=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$. Option B is $|1+i|$, the modulus of the translation part, which has no effect on the scale factor. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\left(x^9-x^3+\dfrac{\tan x}{(1+x^4)^2}\right)dx =$
questions.corrige_markdown: Each term of the integrand is an odd function: $x^9$ and $x^3$ are odd, and $\dfrac{\tan x}{(1+x^4)^2}$ is odd because $\tan x$ is odd and $(1+x^4)^2$ is even. A sum of odd functions is odd, and the integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval $[-1,1]$ is $0$ (the area below the axis cancels the area above). The integrand is also continuous on $[-1,1]$ because $\tan x$ is finite for $|x|\le1<\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}+9x=0$, where $p$ and $q$ are constants, is $x=$
questions.corrige_markdown: The auxiliary equation is $m^2+9=0$, so $m=\pm3i$ (purely imaginary roots, no real part). The general solution is $x=A\cos3t+B\sin3t$, which can be written as a single cosine $x=p\cos(3t+\lambda)$ with $p=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}$ the amplitude and $\lambda$ a phase constant. Options A and B contain $e^{t}$, which would require roots with real part $1$; option D has angular frequency $9$ instead of $\sqrt9=3$. (The printed wording mentions constants $p$ and $q$, but only $p$ and $\lambda$ appear in the options.) **Answer: C.**

themes: mean and root mean square values
questions.enonce_markdown: The mean value of $\cosh2x$ in the interval $0\leq x\leq2$, is
questions.corrige_markdown: The mean value over $[0,2]$ is $\dfrac{1}{2-0}\displaystyle\int_0^2\cosh2x\,dx = \dfrac12\left[\dfrac{\sinh2x}{2}\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{\sinh4}{4}$. Since $\sinh4=\dfrac{e^{4}-e^{-4}}{2}$, the mean value is $\dfrac{e^{4}-e^{-4}}{8}\approx6.82$. Option A forgets the factor $\dfrac12$ from the interval length or from $\sinh$; C and D are far too large. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A curve is given in Cartesian form by the equation $x^2+y^2+2y=(x^2+y^2)^{\frac12}$. The polar equation of the curve is
questions.corrige_markdown: Substitute $x^2+y^2=r^2$, $y=r\sin\theta$ and $(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}=r$ (taking $r>0$): $r^2+2r\sin\theta=r$. Divide by $r\neq0$: $r+2\sin\theta=1$, so $r=1-2\sin\theta$. The presence of $y$ (not $x$) in the term $2y$ forces $\sin\theta$, which eliminates A and C, and the sign comes from moving $2\sin\theta$ to the other side, which eliminates D. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the asymptotes of the hyperbola $\dfrac{x^2}{16}-\dfrac{y^2}{a^2}=1$ are perpendicular, then the value of $a$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The asymptotes of $\dfrac{x^2}{16}-\dfrac{y^2}{a^2}=1$ are $y=\pm\dfrac{a}{4}x$ (obtained from $\dfrac{x^2}{16}-\dfrac{y^2}{a^2}=0$). Two lines are perpendicular when the product of their gradients is $-1$: $\left(\dfrac a4\right)\left(-\dfrac a4\right)=-1$, so $a^2=16$ and $a=4$ (taking $a>0$). This is a rectangular hyperbola, with semi-axes equal. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are two vectors, which one of the following compound statements is true?
questions.corrige_markdown: A: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\varphi$ and $\varphi=90^\circ$ when the vectors are perpendicular, so the dot product is $0$: true. B: for parallel non-zero vectors $\cos\varphi=\pm1$, so the dot product is $\pm|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\neq0$: false. C: take $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}$; then $\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$ although $\mathbf{d}\neq\mathbf{b}$: false. D: $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$ is always perpendicular to $\mathbf{a}$, never parallel to it (unless it is the zero vector): false. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: For what value of $p$ is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}4&3&3\\p&5&6\\6&7&9\end{pmatrix}$ non-invertible?
questions.corrige_markdown: A square matrix is non-invertible exactly when its determinant is $0$. Expanding along the first row: $\det = 4(5\cdot9-6\cdot7)-3(9p-6\cdot6)+3(7p-5\cdot6) = 4(3)-3(9p-36)+3(7p-30) = 12-27p+108+21p-90 = 30-6p$. Setting $30-6p=0$ gives $p=5$. Check: the formula gives $\det=0$ for $p=5$, and for example $\det=-6\neq0$ for $p=6$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A necessary and sufficient condition to show that a group is **NOT** Abelian is
questions.corrige_markdown: Closure, associativity, the existence of an identity and of inverses are the axioms of a group: they hold in every group, Abelian or not, so they can never distinguish a non-Abelian group. What separates the two cases is commutativity: a group is Abelian exactly when $ab=ba$ for all $a,b$, and it is non-Abelian exactly when commutativity fails for at least one pair (for instance in $S_3$, where two transpositions do not commute). Among the options only commutativity is relevant. (The wording 'to show that a group is NOT Abelian' is awkward, but D is the only option that can be meant.) **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution of the system of congruences $x\equiv1\pmod2$, $x\equiv2\pmod3$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Since $\gcd(2,3)=1$, the Chinese remainder theorem gives a unique solution modulo $6$. From $x\equiv1\pmod2$ write $x=1+2k$; then $1+2k\equiv2\pmod3$, so $2k\equiv1\pmod3$ and $k\equiv2\pmod3$ (because $2\times2=4\equiv1$). Then $x=1+2(2+3m)=5+6m$, that is $x\equiv5\pmod6$. Check: $5$ is odd, and $5=3+2$ leaves remainder $2$ on division by $3$. Options A and C are even, and B is a multiple of $3$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solutions of $z^3=-8$ are $z=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Write $-8=8e^{i\pi}$. The cube roots are $z_k=2e^{i(\pi+2k\pi)/3}$ for $k=0,1,2$: $z_0=2e^{i\pi/3}=1+i\sqrt3$, $z_1=2e^{i\pi}=-2$, $z_2=2e^{i5\pi/3}=1-i\sqrt3$. So $z\in\{-2,\ 1\pm i\sqrt3\}$. Check: $(1+i\sqrt3)^3=8e^{i\pi}=-8$. In B and C the complex roots have modulus $\sqrt7$, not $2$; D is the set of cube roots of $+8$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution to the differential equation $4\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}-3\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$ for constants $A$, $B$ is $y=$
questions.corrige_markdown: The auxiliary equation is $4m^2-3m=0$, that is $m(4m-3)=0$, with two distinct real roots $m=0$ and $m=\dfrac34$. The general solution is therefore $y=Ae^{0x}+Be^{\frac34x}=A+Be^{\frac34x}$. Options A and C are the forms for a repeated root, which is not the case here; option D has the reciprocal exponent. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9+x^2}}\,dx=$, where $k$ is a constant, is
questions.corrige_markdown: Standard result: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}=\sinh^{-1}\dfrac xa+k$. Derivation: put $x=3\sinh u$, so $dx=3\cosh u\,du$ and $\sqrt{9+x^2}=3\cosh u$; the integral becomes $\int du=u=\sinh^{-1}\dfrac x3$. Check by differentiation: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sinh^{-1}\dfrac x3=\dfrac{1/3}{\sqrt{1+x^2/9}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9+x^2}}$. The inverse circular functions $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$ belong to $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$, and $\cosh^{-1}$ to $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equation $\dfrac{x^2}{2-a}+\dfrac{y^2}{a-5}=-1$ represents an hyperbola if
questions.corrige_markdown: The conic is a hyperbola when the two denominators have opposite signs, i.e. $(2-a)(a-5)<0$, i.e. $(a-2)(a-5)>0$, i.e. $a<2$ or $a>5$. For $a>5$: $2-a<0$ and $a-5>0$, and the equation becomes $\dfrac{x^2}{a-2}-\dfrac{y^2}{a-5}=1$, a hyperbola. For $2<a<5$ both denominators are negative and the equation becomes $\dfrac{x^2}{a-2}+\dfrac{y^2}{5-a}=1$, an ellipse; options A, B and C all contain values of $a$ in $(2,5)$, so they are not sufficient. Option D is the only one that guarantees a hyperbola (the values $a<2$ also give a hyperbola but are not offered). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\3&2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $N=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&3&1\end{pmatrix}$ are elements of $S_3$, the symmetric group of permutations of $A=\{1,2,3\}$, the composition $M\circ N=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $M\circ N$ means 'apply $N$ first, then $M$'. $N$: $1\to2$, $2\to3$, $3\to1$. $M$: $1\to3$, $2\to2$, $3\to1$. Then $1\xrightarrow{N}2\xrightarrow{M}2$; $2\xrightarrow{N}3\xrightarrow{M}1$; $3\xrightarrow{N}1\xrightarrow{M}3$. So $M\circ N=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&1&3\end{pmatrix}$, the transposition $(1\ 2)$. The other order, $N\circ M$, would give $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\1&3&2\end{pmatrix}$ (option D), which shows that $S_3$ is not Abelian; this is the trap of this question. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the rate at which cells in a certain organism die is inversely proportional to the number $n$, of cells present at time $t$. Treat $n$ as a continuous variable, with $k$, a positive constant. Then, which one of the differential equations is satisfied by $n$?
questions.corrige_markdown: The rate of death is $\dfrac kn$ (inversely proportional to $n$, with proportionality constant $k>0$). Cells are dying, so $n$ decreases and $\dfrac{dn}{dt}$ is negative: $\dfrac{dn}{dt}=-\dfrac kn$. Options C and D have a positive sign (growth), and B has no constant of proportionality ($k$ is given as the positive constant of the model). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Using the approximation $y_{n+1}\cong y_n+2h\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_n$ and a step length of $0.1$, the approximate value of $y$, when $x=1.1$, given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y$ and $y=0$ when $x=1$ is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Take $x_0=1$, $y_0=0$ and $h=0.1$, so one step reaches $x_1=1.1$. At the starting point $\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_0=x_0+y_0=1+0=1$. With the formula prescribed by the question, $y_1\cong y_0+2h\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_0=0+2(0.1)(1)=0.2$. **Answer: D.**

themes: simple harmonic motion of a particle
questions.enonce_markdown: A particle performing SHM has a speed of $v\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ when it is $1\ \mathrm m$ from the centre of oscillations. If the period of oscillations is $\sqrt2\pi\ \mathrm s$, and the amplitude $3\ \mathrm m$, then value of $v$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The angular frequency is $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt2\pi}=\sqrt2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. For SHM, $v^2=\omega^2(a^2-x^2)$ with amplitude $a=3$ and displacement $x=1$: $v^2=2(9-1)=16$, so $v=4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The moment of inertia of a uniform rod of mass $m$ and length $3l$ about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to the rod is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a uniform rod of mass $m$ and length $L$, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular axis through its centre is $\dfrac1{12}mL^2$. Here $L=3l$, so $I=\dfrac1{12}m(3l)^2=\dfrac{9}{12}ml^2=\dfrac34ml^2$. Option B, $\dfrac13ml^2$, is the value about an end of a rod of length $2l$, and option A, $\dfrac14ml^2$, is what one gets from $\dfrac1{12}m(l)^2\times3$: both ignore that the length is $3l$, which must be squared. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A force $\mathbf F=(2\mathbf i-\mathbf j+\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ acts on particle giving it a displacement of $(\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$. The work done by $\mathbf F$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Work is the scalar product of the force and the displacement: $W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf s=(2)(1)+(-1)(1)+(1)(2)=2-1+2=3$. The work done is $3\ \mathrm J$ ($\mathrm{N\,m}$); the unit printed in the options, N, is a misprint for J, but the numerical value $3$ is unambiguous and only option A matches it. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle $P$ moves with constant angular speed $\omega$ on a curve whose polar equation is $r=(1-\cos\theta)$. The traverse component of its acceleration is
questions.corrige_markdown: The transverse component of acceleration is $a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta$. The angular speed is constant, so $\dot\theta=\omega$ and $\ddot\theta=0$. Differentiating $r=1-\cos\theta$: $\dot r=\sin\theta\,\dot\theta=\omega\sin\theta$. Hence $a_\theta=2(\omega\sin\theta)(\omega)=2\omega^2\sin\theta$. Options A and B have the wrong dimension (an acceleration is proportional to $\omega^2$), and the calculation gives a positive sign, which eliminates D. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The coefficient of restitution $e$ of two colliding objects satisfies the inequality
questions.corrige_markdown: The coefficient of restitution is the ratio of the speed of separation to the speed of approach along the line of centres. The limiting case $e=0$ is a perfectly inelastic collision (the bodies stick together or do not rebound) and $e=1$ is a perfectly elastic collision (no loss of kinetic energy); both are allowed. Hence $0\leq e\leq1$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of $k$ for which $p(x)=\begin{cases}k(x+2), & 0\leq x\leq4\\0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$ is a probability density function is
questions.corrige_markdown: A probability density function must be non-negative and integrate to $1$. $\displaystyle\int_0^4k(x+2)\,dx=k\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+2x\right]_0^4=k(8+8)=16k$. Setting $16k=1$ gives $k=\dfrac1{16}$, which also makes $p(x)\geq0$ on $[0,4]$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A liquid is filling a container at the rate of $\dfrac2x$ litres per second where $x$ is the quantity in litres, of liquid in the container after time $t$ seconds. $10$ litres are initially found in the container. How many litres will be found in the container after $75$ seconds?
questions.corrige_markdown: The rate of filling gives $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac2x$, a separable equation: $x\,dx=2\,dt$. Integrating, $\dfrac{x^2}{2}=2t+c$. At $t=0$, $x=10$, so $c=50$. At $t=75$: $\dfrac{x^2}{2}=150+50=200$, so $x^2=400$ and $x=20$ (taking the positive root since a quantity of liquid is positive). There are $20$ litres. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x-y$ and $y=1$ when $x=0$, the value of $y$ when $x=0.1$, using a step length of $0.1$ and the approximation $y_{n+1}\cong y_n+2h\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_n$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take $x_0=0$, $y_0=1$, $h=0.1$. Then $\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_0=0-1=-1$, and the prescribed formula gives $y_1\cong y_0+2h\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_0=1+2(0.1)(-1)=0.8$. **Answer: C.**

themes: simple harmonic motion of a particle
questions.enonce_markdown: A particle oscillates through a distance $\dfrac45\ \mathrm m$ on either side of its equilibrium position with period of $4$ seconds. The maximum speed of the particle in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The amplitude is $a=\dfrac45\ \mathrm m$ (the greatest distance from equilibrium) and the angular frequency is $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi}{4}=\dfrac\pi2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. The maximum speed, reached at the equilibrium position, is $v_{max}=a\omega=\dfrac45\times\dfrac\pi2=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\approx1.26\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the moment of inertia of a square lamina of side $a$ and mass $m$ about an axis through its centre and in its plane is $I$, then its moment of inertia about an axis through the midpoint of one edge and perpendicular to the plane of the lamina is
questions.corrige_markdown: By symmetry the moments of inertia about the two perpendicular in-plane axes through the centre are both $I$. By the perpendicular axes theorem (valid for a lamina), the moment of inertia about the axis through the centre perpendicular to the plane is $I+I=2I$. The required axis is parallel to this one and passes through the midpoint of an edge, at distance $\dfrac a2$ from the centre. By the parallel axes theorem, $I_{req}=2I+m\left(\dfrac a2\right)^2=2I+\dfrac14ma^2$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the force $\mathbf F=(5\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ acts through the point with position vector $\mathbf r=(2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+4\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$, then the magnitude of its moment in $\mathrm{N\,m}$ about $\mathbf O$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The moment about the origin is $\mathbf r\times\mathbf F=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\2&3&4\\5&-2&3\end{vmatrix}=(9+8)\mathbf i-(6-20)\mathbf j+(-4-15)\mathbf k=17\mathbf i+14\mathbf j-19\mathbf k$. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{17^2+14^2+19^2}=\sqrt{289+196+361}=\sqrt{846}\approx29.09$, which rounds to $29.1$ (3 s.f.). Option B, $29$, is only a rounding to 2 s.f.; A is the closest value. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle is moving round the polar curve $r=a\sin\theta$ with constant angular velocity $\omega$. The transverse component of its velocity when $\theta=\dfrac\pi6$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The transverse (perpendicular to the radius vector) component of velocity is $v_\theta=r\dot\theta=(a\sin\theta)\,\omega$. At $\theta=\dfrac\pi6$, $\sin\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac12$, so $v_\theta=\dfrac12a\omega$. The trap is option B, which is the radial component: $\dot r=a\cos\theta\,\dot\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2a\omega$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A smooth sphere moving in space impinges on a similar sphere such that its velocity changes from $(2\mathbf i-\mathbf j-3\mathbf k)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to $(3\mathbf i+\mathbf j-\mathbf k)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The direction of the line of centres is
questions.corrige_markdown: The spheres are smooth, so the impulse they exert on each other acts along the line of centres only; the component of velocity perpendicular to the line of centres is unchanged. The change of velocity is therefore parallel to the line of centres: $(3\mathbf i+\mathbf j-\mathbf k)-(2\mathbf i-\mathbf j-3\mathbf k)=\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$. A direction is defined up to sign, and option B, $-\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-2\mathbf k=-(\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$, is parallel to it. A, C and D are not parallel to $\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$ (D is merely the final velocity). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equivalent of $P(|z|<a)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a standard normal variable $z$, $P(|z|<a)=P(-a<z<a)=\Phi(a)-\Phi(-a)$. By symmetry $\Phi(-a)=1-\Phi(a)$, so $P(|z|<a)=\Phi(a)-\left(1-\Phi(a)\right)=2\Phi(a)-1$. Option B is $P(|z|>a)$ (the two tails) and D is a single tail $P(z>a)$. **Answer: C.**
